opus-5.5.text:
Well, the word "tensor" carries a lot of baggage. In mathematics and physics, a tensor is a multilinear object with transformation properties under change of basis: covariant indices, contravariant indices, all that machinery. In deep learning, people use "tensor" more loosely to mean a multidimensional array of numbers. TensorLogic starts from the deep learning sense, but the key insight is something neither of those communities really emphasized: **a tensor is also a relation.**

Take a logical relation like Parent(x, y). You can represent it as a Boolean matrix, with a one wherever x is a parent of y. Now take a rule like "x is a grandparent of z if x is a parent of y and y is a parent of z." That rule is exactly an Einstein summation: you join on y and project it out, then apply a step function to get back to Booleans. So a Datalog rule and a tensor equation are fundamentally the same operation. A database join is a tensor contraction, and projection is summation over an index.

Once you see that, you can write a whole logic program, a whole neural network, or a mixture of both in a single language, where the only construct is the tensor equation. Convolutional nets, transformers, graph neural networks, kernel machines, and probabilistic graphical models all turn out to be short sets of tensor equations. Symbolic AI and deep learning stop being two separate paradigms you have to glue together. They're two regimes of the same thing.

And it goes further. If you replace those Boolean tensors with embeddings, so objects and relations live in a learned vector space, you can do reasoning in embedding space. There's a temperature-like parameter: at zero you get pure deductive reasoning, with no hallucinations, because it's sound like logic. As you raise it, you get analogical, similarity-based generalization, the kind of thing neural nets are good at. So you get the reliability and transparency of logic with the learning and generalization of deep learning, in one framework.

So in mathematics, a tensor is a geometric object. In TensorLogic, it's the common substrate of reasoning and learning. That's the claim I'm making: this could be the language AI has been missing.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the key thing to understand is that in TensorLogic a tensor isn't just an array of numbers that you multiply and add. It's a logical object. The core observation that TensorLogic rests on is that the two most fundamental operations in AI, which people have always thought of as completely different, are actually the same thing. One is the Einstein summation, the tensor contraction that's at the heart of deep learning, where you multiply tensors along shared indices and sum out the rest. The other is the join in relational databases, or equivalently the rule application in logic programming, where you take two relations, match them on their shared variables, and project out the ones you don't need. If you write a logical rule like "X is a grandparent of Z if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z," that's literally an einsum. The relations are Boolean tensors, the variables are the indices, the conjunction is the product, and the existential quantification over Y is the summation.

So once you see that, a tensor stops being just a mathematical object and becomes a representation of knowledge. A Boolean tensor is a relation. A real-valued tensor is a relation with degrees of truth, or probabilities, or embeddings, depending on how you choose to interpret it. And a tensor program, a sequence of these contractions, is simultaneously a neural network and a logic program. That's what I mean when I say it's more than tensors in the mathematical sense. Mathematicians don't ask what a tensor means. In TensorLogic the meaning is the whole point. It lets you take the structure and reasoning that symbolic AI was always good at and the learning and generalization that neural networks are good at, and have them be the same language rather than two systems bolted together.

And there's a practical consequence to that. If you want reliable reasoning, say in a transformer, you can run the same tensor equations with the Boolean semantics and get sound deduction, with no hallucination, because the system can't derive something that doesn't follow. If you want analogical, fuzzy generalization, you relax to continuous values and you get something like embeddings. The knob between those two is just a parameter in the same framework. You can't do that if you think of tensors purely as numerical arrays, because then you've thrown away the logical interpretation that makes the reasoning sound. So TensorLogic is tensors, yes, but tensors with semantics, and that changes everything about what you can build with them.

r002.rationale: It links TensorLogic to logic programming, but does not attribute any external-memory access capability to that component.

r003.rationale: The response describes tensor programs as logic programs, but does not claim they can perform any computation a computer can.

astra-6.text:
Well, tensors by themselves are a representation. They’re multidimensional arrays, and you can perform operations on them, but that doesn’t by itself tell you what those operations mean in terms of knowledge or reasoning. The idea of TensorLogic is to bring together tensor computation and logic in a single language.

Take a relation like “Alice is Bob’s parent.” You can represent the parent relation as a matrix, where an entry tells you whether one person is the parent of another. Now a rule for grandparents—X is a grandparent of Z if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z—becomes a tensor operation. You combine the two relations and sum over that intermediate variable, Y. With Boolean values and the appropriate operations, that’s logical inference.

The interesting thing is that the same basic machinery also expresses neural network computations. So you can write down rules, learn representations, and combine them without having to bolt a symbolic system onto a neural network as two separate things.

That’s the sense in which it’s more than tensors as mathematical objects. The tensors are the substrate; the language gives them a logical interpretation and lets us connect reasoning with learning.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a tensor, by itself, is a mathematical object. It gives you a way to represent quantities and perform operations on them, but it doesn’t tell you what those quantities mean or how to reason with them. The idea of TensorLogic is to bring that representation together with logic.

Think of a relation in a database: “Alice is a friend of Bob.” You can represent that as an entry in a matrix, with one index for Alice and another for Bob. A relation involving more entities becomes a higher-order tensor. Now logical rules become computations over those tensors. You can combine relations, introduce intermediate variables, and derive new relations.

What makes that interesting is that tensor operations are also the language of neural networks. So you have a possible common language for learning and reasoning: you can express structured knowledge and rules, while also working with representations that can be learned from data. The ambition is much broader than using tensors as a convenient mathematical notation. It’s to connect two ways of doing AI that have largely developed separately.
